text: My son, if you accept my words and treasure up my commands within you,
turning your ear toward wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding—
yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding,
if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasure,
then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God.
For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding.
He stores up sound wisdom for the upright; he is a shield to those who walk in integrity,
guarding the paths of justice and watching over the way of his faithful ones.
Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity—every good path.
For wisdom will enter your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul.
Discretion will watch over you, and understanding will guard you,
rescuing you from the way of evil, from those who speak perversely,
from those who abandon the straight paths to walk in ways of darkness,
who delight in doing wrong and rejoice in the perversity of evil,
whose paths are crooked and whose ways are devious.
It will also rescue you from the forbidden woman, from the stranger who makes her words smooth,

versions.text: It will rescue you also from the adulteress, from the stranger with her smooth words,
versions.explanation: The Hebrew 'ishshah zarah' means the 'strange' or 'forbidden' woman, not specifically an 'adulteress'; the broader term keeps the range of meaning intended in the chapter. Also, 'hechelikah' is a verb ('she makes her words smooth/flatters'), which is better rendered actively.

versions.text: It will rescue you also from the forbidden woman, from the stranger who flatters with smooth words,
versions.explanation: Two small gains: moving 'also' before the verb reads more smoothly aloud than the interrupted 'rescue you also'; and the Hebrew has the possessive 'her words' (אֲמָרֶיהָ), which the generic 'smooth words' loses. Keeping the verb active ('makes her words smooth') preserves the earlier correction while restoring the pronoun.

text: who forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God.
For her house sinks down to death, and her paths lead to the shades.<f>The 'shades' (Hebrew: rephaim) are the departed spirits of the dead.</f>

versions.text: For her house sinks down to death, and her paths lead to the shades.
versions.explanation: 'The shades' is accurate but obscure to most hearers; a brief footnote clarifies the Hebrew term without altering the poetic line.

text: None who go to her return, nor do they reach the paths of life.
So that you may walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous.

versions.text: So you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous.
versions.explanation: 'Lema'an' introduces a purpose clause, which completes the thought of the preceding verses; 'so that you may walk' captures the intent better than a simple future statement.

text: For the upright will dwell in the land, and those of integrity will remain in it,
but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous torn away from it.
